length: 3 weeks · 6 core lessons and the topic test, plus optional Lesson 4 and above-level Lessons 8–10
description: Students model the Earth–Sun–Moon system to explain day and night, seasons, the Moon’s phases, eclipses and tides, then move out into the solar system. They evaluate the benefits, risks and sustainability of space technology, and study Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander astronomy as science built over tens of thousands of years of observation on Country. Lessons 8–10 take a ready class above level: the search for life, gravity and orbits, and stars and starlight.
notes: **Lesson 4 (Reading the Rocks) is optional** — the unit is coherent without it, and §3 is not assessed.
**Lessons 8–10 sit above the Year 7 level** — the core unit is complete without them; run them with a ready class or as individual extension.
**No practicals in this unit yet.** {{PH:Add a practical (e.g. modelling Moon phases with a lamp and ball, or crater formation) or the 2027 Observatory / Planetarium excursion, with RiskAssess}}

achievement.text: Explain how cyclic changes in the relative positions of Earth, the Sun and the Moon cause predictable phenomena on Earth, including day and night, seasons, the Moon’s phases, eclipses and tides.
Organise data in tables, graphs, models and mathematical relationships; analyse patterns, trends and anomalies.

Explain how new evidence can change scientific models (models of the solar system); examine how different perspectives and worldviews contribute to scientific knowledge (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander astronomy); discuss the considerations in responses to a socio-scientific issue (space debris); analyse how science communication shapes viewpoints, policies and regulations.

descriptors.text: Cyclic changes in the relative positions of Earth, the Sun and the Moon cause eclipses and predictable phenomena on Earth, including seasons and tides
Scientific knowledge, including models and theories, can change because of new evidence
Multidisciplinary endeavours to advance scientific knowledge draw on people’s different perspectives and worldviews
Proposed scientific responses to socio-scientific issues impact society and involve ethical, environmental, social and economic considerations
Science communication shapes individual viewpoints, community policies and regulations
Rock-cycle processes occur over different timescales; rock properties reflect their formation — Lesson 4 (optional) only
Science inquiry — organising data in tables, graphs, models and mathematical relationships (I04); analysing patterns, trends and anomalies (I05)
Balanced and unbalanced forces, including gravitational force — the Year 7–8 entry point for Lesson 9
Levels 9–10, above level — space exploration and the challenges of living away from Earth
Levels 9–10, above level — galaxies, stars, solar systems and black holes; the big bang theory
Levels 9–10, above level — wave models and the electromagnetic spectrum
Levels 9–10, above level — Newton’s laws applied to orbits

prepare: Lesson 1 entry task: rank Earth, Moon, Sun and other objects by size.
Every deck from Lesson 2 opens with a spaced retrieval warm-up.
review: Booklet sections checked in class; Stile check-ins; exit passes.
The [Retrieval Quiz](quiz.html) — 217 questions, filter by lesson — for revision.
diff: Structure tasks in §1 are label-the-diagram rather than blank recall; phases are taught from the visualiser before the diagram; planet mnemonics on the slide.
The milestone task is cut-and-arrange; the debris calculation comes with the formula and one worked substitution.
Revision runs off the Retrieval Quiz filtered to the weakest lessons.
extension: Lessons 8–10 (above level, VC2S10U12–U14, U17), behind the violet divider in the booklet.
Lesson 7 *You do*: reply to “Aboriginal astronomy can’t be reliable science because it isn’t written down”; the Lesson 6 mission brief.

lessons.title: Earth, Moon and Sun
li: Describe the relative sizes of Earth, Moon and Sun.
Explain Earth’s layered structure.
Calculate light travel times.
sc: I can rank Earth, Moon and Sun by size, name Earth’s four layers, and work out how long light takes to travel between them.
guided: Booklet §1 — [pp. 3–7](booklet/Space_Unit_Booklet_Yr7_8.pdf#page=3) (or the [Lesson 1 print](booklet/Space_Lesson1_Print.pdf))
*You do*: light-travel-time calculations
**Stile:** Introduction — Journey to the Sun
review: Exit pass — name Earth’s four layers

lessons.title: Day, night and seasons
li: Distinguish rotation from revolution.
Describe how axial tilt causes seasons; identify solstices and equinoxes.
sc: I can explain why Australia has summer in December.

prac.name: The angle of sunlight — a torch on grid paper at 90° to 15°, measuring the area of the light patch
prac.si: Measure precisely, repeat each angle, and draw a line graph with a line of best fit (VC2S8I02, VC2S8I04, VC2S8I05).
prac.su: Explain why the ground heats more in summer, when the Sun is higher, using axial tilt (VC2S8U12).

guided: Booklet §2.1–§2.3 — [pp. 8–10](booklet/Space_Unit_Booklet_Yr7_8.pdf#page=8)
**Stile:** 0.2 Day and night · 2.1 Seasons · 2.3 Daylight hours

lessons.title: Moon phases and tides
li: Explain what causes the Moon’s phases and sequence the eight phases.
Explain how the Moon and Sun cause tides; distinguish spring from neap tides; explain eclipses.
sc: I can name the eight phases in order and tell spring tides from neap tides using the positions of Sun, Earth and Moon.
explicit: [Lesson 3 · The Moon — Phases & Tides](deck3.html) slides — interactive phase visualiser (Southern Hemisphere by default)
guided: Booklet §2.4–§2.5 — [pp. 11–13](booklet/Space_Unit_Booklet_Yr7_8.pdf#page=11)
**Stile:** 3.1 The phases of the Moon · 3.2 Eclipses · 3.4 Tides
review: **Stile check-ins:** The phases of the Moon, Eclipses, Tides

lessons.title: Reading the Rocks
li: Explain how a layered rock records the tides; interpret the Elatina data table.
Explain tidal braking; describe the evidence that dates the Acraman impact.
sc: I can state what one lamina in a rhythmite represents, and name two rock features only an impact produces.
explicit: [Lesson 4 · Reading the Rocks](deck4.html) slides — runs from the deck’s photographs and the Elatina data table
guided: Booklet §3 — [pp. 14–19](booklet/Space_Unit_Booklet_Yr7_8.pdf#page=14)
Optional: skip it and the sequence still runs
review: Booklet p. 17 worth collecting — §3 is not assessed

lessons.title: Our solar system
li: Order the eight planets; classify terrestrial and giant planets.
Describe dwarf planets, asteroids and comets; use the astronomical unit.
Explain how models of the solar system changed with new evidence (VC2S8H01).
sc: I can list the planets in order from memory and use AU to compare distances.

prac.name: Impact craters — a marble dropped into flour and cocoa from 25 to 100 cm
prac.si: Measure crater diameters to the nearest mm, average repeat drops, spot anomalies and draw a line of best fit (VC2S8I02, VC2S8I04, VC2S8I05, VC2S8I06).
prac.su: Explain how impact speed affects crater size, and why the Moon has more craters than Earth (VC2S8U12).

guided: Booklet §4 — [pp. 20–21](booklet/Space_Unit_Booklet_Yr7_8.pdf#page=20) (planet-order entry task, AU distances)
**Stile:** 1.1 The Solar System · 1.6 Changing models of the Solar System · 1.5 Skill builder — Rounding
review: **Stile check-ins:** The Solar System, Changing models of the Solar System

lessons.title: Space technology and sustainability
li: Outline key milestones in space exploration; describe crewed, robotic and telescope missions and Australia’s contributions.
Explain how space debris accumulates and the Kessler syndrome; evaluate the sustainability of orbital activity (VC2S8H03).
Explain how communicating the science of space debris shapes public views and space regulations (VC2S8H04).
sc: I can evaluate the benefits and risks of a space mission, and propose a debris-management response with its trade-offs.
explicit: [Lesson 6 · Space Technology & Sustainability](deck6.html) slides — two parts
guided: Booklet §5 — [pp. 22–27](booklet/Space_Unit_Booklet_Yr7_8.pdf#page=22): milestone card sort (p. 22), debris kinetic-energy calculation (p. 24)
*You do*: Europa mission design brief, then a debris-management design for the Australian Space Agency

lessons.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander astronomy
li: Explain what dark constellations are; describe the Boorong star catalogue and its significance.
Explain sky knowledge as an ecological calendar and as navigation; recognise it as science developed over 65,000 years.
sc: I can describe dark constellations using the Emu in the Sky, and give an example of Aboriginal knowledge and Western science working together.
explicit: [Lesson 7 · Aboriginal & Torres Strait Islander Astronomy](deck7.html) slides
guided: Booklet §6 — [pp. 28–31](booklet/Space_Unit_Booklet_Yr7_8.pdf#page=28): tracing the Emu in the Sky (p. 28), seasonal calendars, the SKA on Wajarri Country
CSIRO video: the SKA and the Wajarri Yamatji land use agreement

lessons.title: Topic test
li: Show what I know about the Earth–Sun–Moon system, the solar system, space technology and Aboriginal astronomy.
sc: I can answer questions from §1, §2, §4, §5 and §6 under test conditions.
guided: Revision from the [Retrieval Quiz](quiz.html) filtered to the weakest lessons
Stile *Test: The Solar System* is a ready-made alternative paper
review: **CAT — Summative:** end-of-unit written assessment on §1, §2, §4, §5 and §6 (§3 excluded)
Booklet marked from the [Solution Set](solutions.html) (staff password)

lessons.title: The search for life
li: Describe the conditions needed for life and the habitable zone.
Describe promising targets in our solar system; explain how exoplanets are detected.
sc: Above level — stretch, not a pass/fail line.
guided: Booklet §7 — [pp. 33–37](booklet/Space_Unit_Booklet_Yr7_8.pdf#page=33): conditions-for-life sort
*You do*: a scientific argument for life in Europa’s subsurface ocean
review: Formative only — evidences above-standard work for reporting

lessons.title: Gravity and orbits
li: State Newton’s law of universal gravitation.
Explain what an orbit is and why orbiting objects don’t fall; relate altitude to orbital speed and period.
sc: Above level — stretch, not a pass/fail line.
guided: Booklet §8 — [pp. 38–41](booklet/Space_Unit_Booklet_Yr7_8.pdf#page=38): Newton’s cannonball (p. 39), geostationary orbit
**Stile:** 1.2 The role of gravity — a bridge into this lesson

lessons.title: Stars, galaxies and starlight
li: Light-years, star types and stellar life cycles, galaxies.
The electromagnetic spectrum, telescopes and spectroscopy.
sc: Above level — stretch, not a pass/fail line.
explicit: [Lesson 10 · Stars, Galaxies & Starlight](deck10.html) slides — two parts
guided: Booklet §9 — [pp. 42–47](booklet/Space_Unit_Booklet_Yr7_8.pdf#page=42): light-year scaling table, ordering the EM spectrum, choosing a telescope
